items.title: 'Trump Needs a Way Out of This War': Michel Yakovleff explains 'charade' over US-Iran negotiations
items.summary:
Eve Irvine is pleased to welcome General Michel Yakovleff, Professor at Sciences-Po and Former Vice-Chief of Staff at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape).. He presents a strategic rather than tactical reading of the current lull in the US-Iran conflict. He argues that the apparent de-escalation is not evidence of diplomatic progress but of mounting structural constraints. Rather than viewing pauses in hostilities as signs of imminent peace, he frames them as consequences of political pressure, military logistics and industrial limitations.
 
At the centre of his argument is the proposition that modern warfare is ultimately governed by sustainability. Missile stockpiles, industrial production capacity, domestic political legitimacy and alliance commitments become as decisive as battlefield success. General Yakovleff contends that the United States retains ample military capability to continue operations against Iran in isolation, yet doing so progressively erodes its ability to deter other adversaries, reassure allies and sustain global commitments.

items.title: Syria walks a tightrope as war engulfs the Middle East
items.summary: Syria has so far avoided becoming a battlefield in the U.S.-Israel-Iran crisis, but it has not escaped the consequences. As regional peace remains elusive, Syria is confronting the challenge of rebuilding following years of gruesome civil war while shielding its fragile recovery from a new wave of geopolitical turmoil. The relatively new Syrian government has prioritized reconstruction, foreign investment, and institution rebuilding. However, the expanding crisis has already created economic and security pressures through trade disruptions, investor uncertainty, and new refugee flows. Higher transportation and insurance costs, along with increased caution among investors, threaten to slow Syria’s recovery just as the country seeks to move beyond its long civil war. Making matters worse is the fact that most Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states’ economies are experiencing contraction as a result of the Iran war, meaning that their earlier economic memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and agreements with Damascus are likely to be cut back, if not eliminated. clusters.headline: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace

items.title: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace
items.summary: For more than two decades, endless wars have destabilized the Middle East, creating huge amounts of human suffering, displacement and trauma. The region is exhausted, with little faith in the possibility of peace and few structures to enable it. The region is now at an inflection point; it can continue endless violence or undertake serious mediation and conflict resolution. The war with Iran has exposed the limits of U.S. military power, leaving only one practical option on the table: pursuing negotiations that recognize the balance of power in the region and the security concerns of all parties. This requires very careful engagement and mediation. There are multiple overlapping conflicts and rivalries within the region. Breaking this cycle requires more than another round of emergency diplomacy; it requires permanent structures for mediation and peacemaking. items.title: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
items.summary: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran, suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II. The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions. These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems. Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation. This comes amid news that the U.S. has burned through other key weapons systems since war with Iran began. items.title: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources
items.summary: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources The US army has used up much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during its five-month war on Iran, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. The US has used "virtually all" munitions for surface-to-surface weapons (ATACMS), and around half of its global Tomahawk supply, the sources said. ATACMS are crucial to allow accurate strikes from a safe distance, and have been widely used by Ukraine against Russia. A person with knowledge of the data said the US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, had burned through nearly all the land-based missiles it had before the war began, and had to resupply from other areas of the world.

items.summary: IRGC says missiles destroyed three US F-35 jets at Jordan base Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it fired several ballistic missiles at Jordan’s al-Azraq airbase, which hosts US F-35 fighter jets. The IRGC said the attack targeted a runway and maintenance hangar in response to a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island that killed two parents and their child, the Fars news agency reported. It said the missiles completely destroyed three F-35 aircraft and inflicted “heavy damage” on three others. The IRGC also said the attack killed several officers and members of the base’s technical and maintenance teams. “A number of enemy officers and technical and maintenance personnel were also killed in this attack. Our region is no place for the infanticidal army that cruelly slaughters innocent families in the middle of the night while they sleep,” it said. The group said its struggle, alongside Jordan’s, would continue until “the last American occupier is expelled from the Islamic lands”.

items.title: US awards Lockheed Martin $58.6bn Patriot missile contract
items.summary: US awards Lockheed Martin $58.6bn Patriot missile contract The US Army has awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6bn to expand production of Patriot interceptor missiles, the Reuters news agency reported. The seven-year agreement will run from the 2026 financial year until 2032 as Washington seeks to rebuild weapons stockpiles depleted by its war on Iran and military support for Ukraine. The deal replaces a one-year contract worth $4.7bn that the army issued in April. It establishes a long-term procurement programme for PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, which target aircraft and ballistic and cruise missiles.

items.summary: Trump hails late US Senator Lindsey Graham as 'true American original' World leaders gathered in Washington, DC, on Tuesday for the funeral ceremony for late Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham, who was instrumental in advocating for the war on Iran and a staunch supporter of Israel. Among those attending were Ukrainian President Zelensky and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. Delivering remarks at the ceremony, Trump called Graham a "beloved friend" and "a true American original". "He never saw a war that he didn’t like," Trump said, drawing laughter before adding that Graham supported military power "for the good of our country." "Above all, Lindsey Graham believed in a strong America," Trump said. "He had unwavering faith in the righteousness of American power." items.summary: US treasury secretary says Hormuz deal with Iran could happen 'today or tomorrow' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the US could reach a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Wednesday, adding that this would stabilise energy prices. "We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC. He was optimistic about the impact a deal with Iran over the strait would have on energy prices, where he said hundreds of ships are waiting to pass. "Even though things are still a little dicey there over the past few days, we've [seen] quite a few ships coming out even now," Bessent said. "So, you know, I'd expect the energy prices to settle back down, which, as I said, will be good for the entire world."

items.title: Most Americans say Iran war isn't worth fighting
Support for Israeli-US war on Iran falls as most Americans call it pointless
items.summary: Support for Israeli-US war on Iran falls as most Americans call it pointless Public backing in the United States for the war on Iran has continued to weaken, a new poll has found. About two-thirds of US adults said the conflict which Israel pushed the country in to had no purpose and was not worth pursuing, the survey by the Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research showed. The findings also indicated declining support for President Donald Trump’s decision to wage war, with few respondents favouring a prolonged conflict. Only two in 10 adults supported continuing US military operations against Iran. Three in 10 said Washington should halt its attacks and pursue another ceasefire through negotiations. The results point to growing public opposition as the war continues to drain US military resources, increase fuel costs, and destabilise the wider Middle East.

items.summary: Egypt says drone attack sparked fire on American LNG ships Egypt has attributed a fire that damaged two vessels at the Mediterranean port of Damietta to a drone attack, marking its first official account of Wednesday’s incident. The Egyptian cabinet said preliminary findings showed that a drone caused the 29 July blaze. No group has taken responsibility. Authorities have opened an investigation into the circumstances of the attack, citing the need to defend Egypt’s national security and interests. Maritime security company Ambrey said the drone struck a US-owned floating gas storage tanker before flames spread to a second vessel. Officials reported no casualties. Egypt’s Petroleum Ministry had previously confirmed the fire but did not identify its cause. The attack has raised fears that the regional war could spread further after Iran targeted US-linked interests in several countries. If confirmed as part of the wider conflict, it would represent the first attack of its kind on Egyptian territory since the war began.

items.summary: Iran threatens Hormuz ban on countries accepting frozen assets under Trump plan Iran has warned that it will bar countries and companies from the Strait of Hormuz if they receive money drawn from frozen Iranian assets. US President Donald Trump earlier proposed using Tehran’s blocked funds to cover damage to ships and cargo in the waterway. Iran denounced the proposal as “incendiary”. Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, which oversees the unified command of the country’s armed forces, said the restrictions would apply to “All companies and countries that welcome Trump’s proposal and use Iran’s blocked assets”. The command described Trump’s threat as an “illegal action.”

items.summary: Iran executes two men over charges related to January protests Iran has executed two men who were sentenced to death for their part in protests in Isfahan during nationwide unrest that rocked the country in January, the Judiciary's Mizan News Agency reported on Tuesday. Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi were among 12 men sentenced to death on charges of taking part in the killing of security force members in Alikhani Square in Isfahan on January 8. Another two in the same trial had already been executed. Reporting by Reuters

clusters.headline: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war

items.title: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war
items.summary: In recent weeks, Iran has gone on the offensive, striking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and launching a surprise attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. From a distance, these moves look like self-defeating escalation. Why should a badly damaged state, under severe economic pressure, lash out at the U.S. instead of pushing for a ceasefire? The answer, simply put, is that Iran is digging in for a long war. Whatever Washington's intentions, Tehran increasingly interprets sanctions, negotiations, temporary ceasefires and military strikes as different instruments aimed at a single objective: regime change. As long as this primary objective remains, Iran expects no sanctions relief or meaningful de-escalation. My conversations with Iranian foreign policy analysts suggest that Tehran now believes the war will continue in different forms until the end of Donald Trump's presidency. items.title: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report
items.summary: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report US President Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical shortage of munition during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported. According to the newspaper citing sources, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week after finding out about the deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles. The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100% fake news", adding that Trump saying "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

items.summary: Oorlogsmoe was Amerika, na decennia van 'forever wars', de langdurige strijd van het Amerikaanse leger in andere landen, zoals in Vietnam en Afghanistan. Toch is het de president die beloofde daar een einde aan te maken, die nu de zesde maand ingaat van zijn oorlog met Iran. De onvrede onder Amerikanen groeit. Ook in Middletown, de stad in Ohio waar vicepresident JD Vance werd geboren. "Het stuitert alle kanten op, we hebben geen duidelijk doel", verzucht veteraan John Cox. Hij is gepensioneerd sergeant eerste klasse en diende in Vietnam. "Toen was het idee ook dat we er snel in en ook weer uit zouden gaan." Die oorlog zou uiteindelijk negentien jaar duren. Zo lang loopt de oorlog met Iran nog niet. Maar bij Post 218, een organisatie voor veteranen in Middletown, is er weinig begrip voor de wispelturigheid van Donald Trump. "De ene dag noemt hij het een oorlog, dan weer een schermutseling", zegt Cox aan de bar van Post 218, een soort clubhuis voor veteranen. "Wij horen geen land te zijn dat steeds van koers verandert. Wij moeten ergens naartoe gaan, de klus klaren en weer vertrekken.

items.summary: Questions continue to swirl around the flash flood of nearly 60,000 migrants who swam or walked from Morocco into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Africa last week. How did so many migrants manage to breach Moroccan border security forces, who appear to have largely disappeared from their stations? Why had so many migrants received social media messages encouraging them to swarm the enclave? Analysts pointed their fingers at the Moroccan government, arguing it was once again deploying “migration blackmail,” as the practice has been dubbed, to punish its European neighbors and bend them to its will. But this time, Israel and the United States appear to be the principal beneficiaries. Indeed, they have seized on the politically embarrassing episode to weaken a Spanish government they view as one of their principal European antagonists. This was not the first time Ceuta’s border had been breached, nor the first time that Morocco was accused of opening its borders to allow streams of migrants to enter European territory. The state-owned Saudi Arabian oil giant’s adjusted net income rose to $33.4bn from $25.2bn a year ago. The second quarter runs from early April to the end of June. The US and Iran reached a ceasefire in April that was extended in June, but fighting has continued to rage, keeping energy prices inflated. Iran is attempting to assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked dozens of vessels trying to transit the strait via Oman’s territorial waters. The US has bombarded Iran, and in response, Tehran has targeted Gulf states, particularly Kuwait and Bahrain. The war drove Brent, the international benchmark, up above $100 per barrel in May and then again in July. Prices for refined products, like diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline, are up substantially. clusters.headline: Israel-Lebanon negotiations 'stalling': 'Situation on ground far from spirit of framework agreement'

items.title: Israel-Lebanon negotiations 'stalling': 'Situation on ground far from spirit of framework agreement'
items.summary: Carys Garland is pleased to welcome Joseph BAHOUT, Director, Issam Fares Institute for Public Policy & International Affairs. Despite the symbolism of a seventh round of US-sponsored negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, Bahout argues that the process is increasingly characterised by stagnation rather than diplomatic momentum. He suggests that the core obstacles are no longer merely technical disagreements over the implementation of the June framework agreement, but a convergence of military realities, domestic political constraints, diminishing American engagement, and wider regional tensions. The negotiations, in his view, exist within a broader strategic ecosystem in which progress on Lebanese-Israeli arrangements remains contingent upon developments in the Iran-US war and Israeli domestic politics.

items.title: Iraq exported under a third of pre-war oil levels via Hormuz in July: monitor
items.summary: Iraq exported under a third of pre-war oil levels via Hormuz in July: monitor Iraq exported less than a third of its pre-war oil levels in July through the Strait of Hormuz, data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler showed on Tuesday. Before the US-Israeli war on Iran began, Iraq was exporting on average 105 million barrels per month through Hormuz, while only around 30 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil were able to pass through the waterway between 4 July and 4 August, according to vessels detected by Kpler.

items.title: El Ibex 35 cierra por encima de los 20.000 puntos por primera vez en su historia
items.summary: El Ibex 35 ha derribado en la sesión de este martes 4 de agosto la barrera de los 20.000 puntos tras abrir el día con un incremento del 0,09%. Un movimiento mínimo que le ha permitido alcanzar esta cota en los primeros compases de la mañana y que supone un nuevo máximo histórico para la cotización del selectivo español. A media mañana ha vuelto a quedar por debajo porque se ha dado la vuelta a rojo de forma mínima y por la tarde ha recuperado el pulso. Lo cierto es que la trayectoria del Ibex lleva en tendencia ascendente desde que se terminó la pandemia de Covid-19, allá por 2023. Desde entonces, el selectivo español ha encadenado años al alza, especialmente en 2024 y 2025. De hecho este año pasado se apuntó un alza del 50%, impulsado principalmente por los bancos, que tienen mucho peso en el conjunto del índice. Y la tendencia ha continuado este 2026, aunque de momento de manera algo más contenida, con un incremento de algo más del 14% desde principios de año. clusters.headline: Robert Kagan: Sometimes US intervention is worth blowback

items.title: Robert Kagan: Sometimes US intervention is worth blowback
items.summary: Robert Kagan surprised some people. One of America’s most influential hawks condemned the Trump administration’s botched war in Iran, suggesting in The Atlantic in March that U.S. involvement in the Middle East has been a catalyst of, rather than a prudent response to, Islamic terrorism. A senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and prolific historian, Kagan has advocated U.S. primacy for decades, starting with his support for Nicaragua’s Contra insurgents as the head of the State Department’s Office of Public Diplomacy (1985-88). In 1997, Kagan co-founded Project for the New American Century, a neoconservative think tank that lobbied for a muscular foreign policy and the maintenance of U.S. global hegemony. The group exercised its considerable influence to push regime change in Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. Kagan’s advocacy has always been based on a belief that the world would collapse into disorder without American leadership, even though U.S. military misadventures have repeatedly destabilized parts of the world. items.title: US is the real loser if Senate passes virtue signaling Russia sanctions
items.summary: As the Senate returns to Washington for its last week in session until mid-September, it faces a long to-do list. But for many senators, the top priority is not enacting legislation that will help Americans but instead rushing to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 , known colloquially as the “Russia sanctions bill.” A passion project of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The legislation’s backers hope that, by choking off funding for Russia’s war effort, they can force Moscow to make greater concessions in ongoing negotiations to end the four-year old conflict in Ukraine. But this logic and the bill itself are fundamentally flawed. The new legislation will have a limited effect on Russia’s fortunes; as has been the case since the beginning of the war, additional economic punishments are unlikely to be decisive in Putin’s calculus. items.summary: Report: Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran The Trump administration seems to be struggling to figure out how to get out of its self-made Iran quagmire. According to a CNN report on Monday, the US military is now crowdsourcing ideas among military experts for what to do next in order to push Iran into a deal that is to President Donald Trump's liking. "We are looking for new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran," an email from an officer in US Central Command's (Centcom) intelligence branch read last week, according to the CNN report. A Centcom spokesperson said the move is not unusual, and that it "has a long history of thinking and working in innovative ways". But the email suggests the Pentagon did not plan for the conflict to drag out this long. Read more: Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran: Report

items.summary: Oil prices drop following Trump announcement on Iran talks Crude oil futures fell over six percent after President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would begin imminently to end the war, although Iran denies any such talks are taking place. The drop in oil prices boosted US stocks at the opening, with Dow Jones jumping 1.3 percent, Nasdaq up 1.2 percent, and the broader S&P 500 up 0.9 percent. items.summary: Those who anticipated that a U.S. war against Iran would risk igniting a region-wide conflagration are looking prescient. The latest metastasis of the conflict has included airstrikes by both the United States and Saudi Arabia in Iraq, against Iraqi militias seen as allied with Iran. The Houthi regime in Yemen, as a direct outgrowth of the U.S.-Iran war, has renewed attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. This has led to new fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which is preparing a possible new offensive in Yemen and is attempting to draw in dozens of other countries on its side of this fray. The Iranian strategy of responding to the U.S. and Israeli aggression through horizontal escalation has drawn in still more countries. Iranian strikes against Saudi Arabia and the UAE have led to Saudi and Emirati attacks in Iran. Other Iranian retaliatory strikes have occurred in Kuwait , Bahrain , Qatar , and Jordan , scene of the most recent American casualties. clusters.headline: Fox News screaming desperately into wind as Trump loses grip

items.title: Fox News screaming desperately into wind as Trump loses grip
items.summary: Fox News has always served as a purveyor of Republican war propaganda, but its coverage of the Iran conflict has been particularly aggressive, and in many ways unmoored from reality, giving their viewers a more than skewed vision of what President Donald Trump can — and cannot — accomplish in Iran today. It appears that it has been an editorial decision at Fox to convince their audience (whose median age is 55) that the Iranians cannot be negotiated with nor trusted and that war was — and still is — the only option. Its range of hosts and guests continue to insist that Trump’s military campaign has been a rousing success (by all independent, observable accounts it has not) and he just needs to finish the job. Of course this a bit of a far cry from the decisive regime change narrative that Fox had generated in the lead-up to the war. items.summary: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history It’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hosts reimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist rule after regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword for ill-considered western interventionism and nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase first coined during Vietnam . If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. clusters.headline: The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi

items.title: The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi
items.summary: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow The US war against Iran is spiraling out of control. Over the past week, the conflict has expanded across the Middle East , with attacks and counterattacks in at least five other countries. Instead of a quick war that sought to topple Iran’s regime, Donald Trump has started a regional conflict that risks severely disrupting energy supplies and prices – and triggering a global recession. After a few days of relative calm, the conflict resumed with the Pentagon carrying out almost nightly strikes against Iran, and Tehran retaliating against US military bases in the region. The conflict also extended to attacks in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan and Egypt. And there’s little sign that peace negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being brokered by Pakistan and Qatar, are making much progress. Continue reading...

items.title: Kpler says Hormuz traffic drops sharply, remains steady through Bab el-Mandeb
items.summary: Kpler says Hormuz traffic drops sharply, remains steady through Bab el-Mandeb Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped sharply, with vessel crossings falling 77 percent day-on-day to just five ships, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler. Kpler said all recorded transits used the Iranian Unilateral Scheme, indicating reduced operational confidence and limited routing options through the strategic waterway. By contrast, traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb remained relatively steady, with 47 vessel crossings despite continued movements by sanctioned ships, shadow fleet activity, and one dark transit. "With US and Iranian public positions still at odds, operators are closely monitoring traffic volumes, routing behaviour and any diplomatic developments that could reshape risk across regional shipping lanes in the days ahead," Kpler said. Hormuz traffic drops sharply The latest maritime risk data points to growing divergence across the region's two strategic chokepoints. items.title: Biosecurity Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: As part of its coverage of disruptive technologies that might come to pose global-scale threats, the Bulletin publishes articles on all the ways in which emerging science and technology can affect biological risks. COVID-19 highlighted those risks and led to voluminous coverage of the pandemic and related subjects, including gain-of-function research that could create potentially dangerous new pathogens that might, if accidentally released, spark a disease outbreak. But we also attempt to answer a wide variety of biosecurity- and biosafety-related questions: Are the laboratories used to study pathogens as safe and secure as they need to be? Will artificial intelligence make it easier and simpler for bad actors to develop or use biological weapons? Will efforts at human enhancement spark arms races or exacerbate societal inequality? Do policies that reduce compulsory vaccination increase the threat of diseases once thought tamed? Can political disinformation about bioweapons disrupt international efforts to minimize threats?

items.title: Nuclear Risk Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: Founded by scientists and engineers of the Manhattan Project in the wake of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists has been alerting humanity to the danger of nuclear catastrophe since December 1945. For 80 years, the Bulletin has relentlessly pursued this mission by informing the public, policymakers, and scientists about new and evolving risks from nuclear technologies. Our authors include the world’s leading experts in the fields of nuclear weapons and their delivery platforms, nuclear security, nuclear safety, and nuclear waste policy. These experts and a staff of editors work together to provide accessible, authoritative articles for policy makers and citizens alike, with the aim of ensuring that nuclear science makes life on Earth better, not worse.

items.title: Trouble in Paris? There's a Gaullist cure for that American hubris
items.summary: Last month, as world leaders prepared to gather in France for the G7 Summit, French officials had Donald Trump on the mind. Using its privileges as host, Paris worked diligently to avoid any hiccups that might upset the U.S. president. First, it delayed the meeting from June 14 to June 16, ensuring that it wouldn’t interfere with Trump’s 80th birthday celebration, or the cage match on the White House lawn that accompanied it. Then, French President Emmanuel Macron went “out of his way” to design an agenda to “appeal to the sort of things Trump wants,” as one analyst told Reuters. Last, and perhaps most bizarrely, French officials delayed the ceremonial transfer of the remains of French Resistance hero Marc Bloch, who was set to be reinterred at France’s illustrious Panthéon in the heart of Paris on June 16. One of the most consequential questions raised by the various bills is whether to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force that has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since 2023, as a terrorist group. clusters.headline: Party elites so blind they can't see their base turning against the war

items.title: Party elites so blind they can't see their base turning against the war
items.summary: Last week, only four House Republicans voted with 210 Democrats to pass a war powers resolution to end the U.S. war with Iran. That means 208 House Republicans voted to continue the war. Hours later, the Republican-led Senate killed the measure, with only one GOP senator voting with the Democrats to end the war, de facto joining four other Republicans who were either absent or missed the vote. The overwhelming majority of congressional Republicans are still clearly committed to President Donald Trump’s war. Republican voters? Not so much. A new Politico poll , published just one day before these votes, revealed a growing gap between congressional Republicans’ continued unqualified support for the war and GOP voters' seeming increasing lack of it. As recently as May, “half of President Donald Trump’s MAGA base thought the Iran war was worth its economic costs” but now barely over a third do, the news outlet reported. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei paid tribute to the second brigadier general after authorities recovered and identified his remains. Kazemi was one of four crew members aboard two Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force Su-24 bombers taking part in an attack on 2 March 2026. Iranian military officials said air defence systems struck the aircraft while they were flying over the Gulf. Baghaei said search operations and identification efforts remained under way for the other three crew members. He announced the funeral processions in a statement on X as mourners gathered to honour Kazemi.

items.summary: IRGC says it downed hostile drone over southwestern Iran Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone over the southwestern port city of Bandar Imam Khomeini early on Thursday. The IRGC’s local division detected the unmanned aircraft inside the city’s airspace before shooting it down, the Tasnim news agency reported. Parts of the drone fell onto a residential property following the interception, but authorities reported no deaths. An IRGC explosives team later secured the wreckage, removed it from the house and neutralised any remaining danger, Tasnim said. The military did not identify the drone’s type, origin or intended target. Bandar Imam Khomeini sits on the Gulf coast in Iran’s Khuzestan province and contains one of the country’s most important commercial ports.

clusters.headline: Trump's Lebanon fantasy is running smack into reality

items.title: Trump's Lebanon fantasy is running smack into reality
items.summary: On June 26, two official delegations — one from Israel and one from Lebanon — signed a framework agreement with great fanfare in Washington. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, openly enthusiastic, framed the event as paving the way toward “lasting peace and security” between Beirut and Tel Aviv. A month later, President Donald Trump received Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House. Once again, Rubio welcomed the visit and reiterated the goal of disarming Hezbollah and achieving a complete and definitive peace between Lebanon and its southern neighbor. Like Tel Aviv, Rubio favors a top-down approach that centers on force and coercion. To neutralize both Tehran and Hezbollah, this camp hopes to combine strong military action against Iranian territory with maximum pressure on the government in Beirut. The goal is two-fold: to strong-arm the Lebanese government into sidelining Hezbollah and to permanently separate the Lebanese and Iranian equations. Within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that this roadmap is the most effective approach. Vice President JD Vance

De drone raakte de opslagtanker Energos Winter en veroorzaakte brand. Die sloeg over naar een ander schip, meldt persbureau Reuters op basis van vijf verschillende bronnen. Beide schepen zouden zijn gebruikt voor de opslag en verwerking van aardgas. Rookpluim De havendienstverlener bevestigt dat er in Damietta brand is uitgebroken op twee gastankers. Op sociale media circuleren beelden van de brand. Daarop is een grote rookpluim te zien boven de stad. Het vuur is inmiddels onder controle. Waar de drone vandaan kwam of wie die lanceerde, is nog onduidelijk. Het is afgelopen dagen weer onrustig in het Midden-Oosten. Zo heeft Iran gisteravond en vanochtend raketaanvallen uitgevoerd op Jordanië . Ook een Amerikaanse legerbasis was doelwit. De Iraanse Revolutionaire Garde heeft de aanvallen opgeëist. clusters.headline: Climate Change Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists

items.title: Climate Change Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: In 1978, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists published a cover story titled “Is mankind warming the Earth?” The answer then, as now, was an “unqualified ‘yes.’” Between July 2023 and June 2024, the average global temperature was over 1.5 degrees Celsius (or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the pre-industrial average, the result of over a century of rampant fossil fuel use and associated greenhouse gas emissions. This warming has resulted in global climate change. The Bulletin covers all aspects of the causes and wide-ranging impacts of this existential crisis, from glacier retreat and sea level rise to drought, extreme weather, and intense wildfires. We also investigate the most promising ways to slow and eventually halt global warming, probing uncertainties and irreversible tipping points in the Earth’s climate and biosphere that threatens all life on Earth.

clusters.headline: Al-Sadr tells Iran-backed groups to keep Iraq out of war

items.title: Al-Sadr tells Iran-backed groups to keep Iraq out of war
items.summary: Al-Sadr tells Iran-backed groups to keep Iraq out of war Influential Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr has urged Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and allied armed groups to stop launching attacks from Iraq. Al-Sadr warned the groups against pulling the country into another conflict and called on Baghdad to assert state control. “Rogue militias must not give our brothers in the Gulf states a pretext to target our sacred land,” he wrote on X. He urged all sides not to “be drawn into the schemes of the Zionist-American enemy to incite brothers to fight and kill one another”. “Iraq and its people need peace,” al-Sadr said, calling for a region free from foreign military bases and colonial domination.

items.summary: Biologists say cargo ships stranded in Gulf may carry highly potent invasive species around the world as trade resumes The closure of the strait of Hormuz has created conditions for an extreme global biodiversity threat, with scientists warning that thousands of stranded ships could spread invasive marine species across the world’s oceans once they begin sailing again. More than 1,500 commercial vessels have been stuck in the Gulf since the strategic waterway closed on 28 February after the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran . An international team of marine biologists said that with the stranded ships remaining motionless, their hulls were becoming encrusted with marine life – from microbes and algae to barnacles and other invertebrates – that could hitchhike to ports around the world when trade resumed. It is not a victory in any conventional military sense: about 3,500 Iranians have been reported killed and the US-led bombing has caused anywhere between $150bn and $270bn of damage . Yet Donald Trump’s decision to pause, rather than intensify, the 13-night summer bombing campaign in effect represents a degree of recognition that the US cannot achieve its stated goals by military power alone. items.title: Iran valt Jordanië aan, VS en Saudi-Arabië bombarderen milities in Irak
items.summary: Iran heeft gisteravond en vanochtend raketaanvallen uitgevoerd op Jordanië. De Jordaanse staatsnieuwszender meldt dat het leger vijf raketten heeft "onderschept en vernietigd". Ook een Amerikaanse legerbasis in Jordanië werd aangevallen. De VS spreekt van een verrassingsaanval en stelt dat alle ballistische raketten zijn onderschept. De Iraanse aanval heeft het einde ingeluid van een gevechtspauze die zeker vier dagen heeft geduurd. In Irak zijn afgelopen nacht bombardementen uitgevoerd. Het Amerikaanse leger heeft daar samen met de strijdkrachten van Saudi-Arabië pro-Iraanse milities aangevallen, zo hebben de twee bondgenoten bekendgemaakt. Het Saudische ministerie van Defensie zegt dat deze aanvallen een vergelding zijn voor droneaanvallen op Saudische energiecentrales van de afgelopen dagen. In de verklaringen van de Amerikaanse en Saudische autoriteiten staat niet vermeld of er een direct verband is met de Iraanse raketaanval op Jordanië, die kort daarvoor werd gemeld. While prices are still well below previous wartime peaks, oil markets are once again under pressure—and things are almost certain to get worse. During the first round of the war, oil prices never reached the calamitous levels predicted by some analysts. This seems to have taught the White House a flawed lesson: that the global oil system is more robust than the doomsayers claim and that a war over the world’s most important energy chokepoint can be fought without a significant energy crisis at home. But this is a dangerous misreading. The relative price stability of the market during the first half of 2026 rested on an inherited stock of buffers accumulated over decades: brimming inventories, untapped strategic reserves, insurance capacity, spare production, and a deep well of consumer tolerance. However, the expanding crisis has already created economic and security pressures through trade disruptions, investor uncertainty, and new refugee flows. Higher transportation and insurance costs, along with increased caution among investors, threaten to slow Syria’s recovery just as the country seeks to move beyond its long civil war. Making matters worse is the fact that most Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states’ economies are experiencing contraction as a result of the Iran war, meaning that their earlier economic memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and agreements with Damascus are likely to be cut back, if not eliminated. items.title: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace
items.summary: For more than two decades, endless wars have destabilized the Middle East, creating huge amounts of human suffering, displacement and trauma. The region is exhausted, with little faith in the possibility of peace and few structures to enable it. The region is now at an inflection point; it can continue endless violence or undertake serious mediation and conflict resolution. The war with Iran has exposed the limits of U.S. military power, leaving only one practical option on the table: pursuing negotiations that recognize the balance of power in the region and the security concerns of all parties. This requires very careful engagement and mediation. There are multiple overlapping conflicts and rivalries within the region. items.title: Nearly 80% of US army's interceptors for a key missile defense system depleted: Report
items.summary: Nearly 80% of US army's interceptors for a key missile defense system depleted: Report The US army has used up nearly 80 percent of its interceptors for a key missile defence system, CNN reported citing several sources familiar with the matter. According to the report, senior US military officials warned that the Pentagon’s munitions stockpile is "dangerously low," with key air defence systems particularly depleted during the war on Iran. The US military exhausted nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared to pre-war figures. Meanwhile, half of its Patriot interceptors were burned through since the start of the war. One source familiar with recent internal Pentagon reports noted that the army used "virtually all" of its highly accurate long-range, surface-to-air weapons in the same period.

items.title: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war
items.summary: In recent weeks, Iran has gone on the offensive, striking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and launching a surprise attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. From a distance, these moves look like self-defeating escalation. Why should a badly damaged state, under severe economic pressure, lash out at the U.S. instead of pushing for a ceasefire? The answer, simply put, is that Iran is digging in for a long war. Whatever Washington's intentions, Tehran increasingly interprets sanctions, negotiations, temporary ceasefires and military strikes as different instruments aimed at a single objective: regime change. As long as this primary objective remains, Iran expects no sanctions relief or meaningful de-escalation. My conversations with Iranian foreign policy analysts suggest that Tehran now believes the war will continue in different forms until the end of Donald Trump's presidency. There is no doubt that the war has punished Iran’s economy. items.title: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report
items.summary: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report US President Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical shortage of munition during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported. According to the newspaper citing sources, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week after finding out about the deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles. The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100% fake news", adding that Trump saying "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

Ook in Middletown, de stad in Ohio waar vicepresident JD Vance werd geboren. "Het stuitert alle kanten op, we hebben geen duidelijk doel", verzucht veteraan John Cox. Hij is gepensioneerd sergeant eerste klasse en diende in Vietnam. "Toen was het idee ook dat we er snel in en ook weer uit zouden gaan." Die oorlog zou uiteindelijk negentien jaar duren. Zo lang loopt de oorlog met Iran nog niet. Maar bij Post 218, een organisatie voor veteranen in Middletown, is er weinig begrip voor de wispelturigheid van Donald Trump. "De ene dag noemt hij het een oorlog, dan weer een schermutseling", zegt Cox aan de bar van Post 218, een soort clubhuis voor veteranen. "Wij horen geen land te zijn dat steeds van koers verandert. items.summary: Oman and Iran appear close to a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially providing both an exit from the current round of fighting and the foundation for a more durable maritime order. Washington should welcome such an agreement—even if it acknowledges a degree of Iranian authority in administering traffic through the strait—because US interest dictates that open and non-discriminatory passage must be given priority over control. The emerging formula would reportedly divide responsibility for the shipping lanes. Vessels entering the Persian Gulf would travel through waters administered by Iran, while outbound traffic would pass through an Omani-administered route. Iran would be notified of departing vessels and, while this has not yet been discussed, Tehran appears open to also ensuring that Oman would be notified of incoming traffic. items.title: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
items.summary: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran, suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II. The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions. These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems. Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation. Despite the symbolism of a seventh round of US-sponsored negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, Bahout argues that the process is increasingly characterised by stagnation rather than diplomatic momentum. He suggests that the core obstacles are no longer merely technical disagreements over the implementation of the June framework agreement, but a convergence of military realities, domestic political constraints, diminishing American engagement, and wider regional tensions. The negotiations, in his view, exist within a broader strategic ecosystem in which progress on Lebanese-Israeli arrangements remains contingent upon developments in the Iran-US war and Israeli domestic politics.

items.title: Oil prices fall amid hopes of US-Iran deal
items.summary: Oil prices fall amid hopes of US-Iran deal Oil prices plunged after Qatar said US-Iran negotiations had resumed, and the US treasury secretary suggested a deal could happen "today or tomorrow". These announcements eased concerns over crude supply disruptions that had sent prices soaring in recent months. The main US oil contract, West Texas Intermediate, dropped five percent to $76.32 a barrel, while the international benchmark Brent North Sea crude fell back below $80 a barrel. US stocks have also performed well since the market opened this morning, with the Dow Jones up 1.3 percent, and the S&P 500 hitting an interday record for the first time since June.

items.title: Iran, Ukraine wars depleted 'virtually all' US long-range missiles: Report
items.summary: Reuters reported this morning that the U.S. has used “virtually all” its long-range precision strike missiles during its war on Iran. Reuters’ sources would not say exactly how many of these surface to surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), the U.S. military has left. This comes amid news that the U.S. has burned through other key weapons systems since war with Iran began. Last week, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated the U.S. has fewer than 827 Patriot missiles, and fewer than 278 THAAD ballistic missile interceptors, in its stockpiles. But the depletion began long ago with the Ukraine war. Since 2022, the U.S. gave weapons to Kyiv at rates faster than it could replace them, including Patriot missile interceptors and an unspecified number of ATACMS. items.title: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources
items.summary: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources The US army has used up much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during its five-month war on Iran, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. The US has used "virtually all" munitions for surface-to-surface weapons (ATACMS), and around half of its global Tomahawk supply, the sources said. ATACMS are crucial to allow accurate strikes from a safe distance, and have been widely used by Ukraine against Russia. A person with knowledge of the data said the US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, had burned through nearly all the land-based missiles it had before the war began, and had to resupply from other areas of the world.

items.title: US treasury secretary says Hormuz deal with Iran could happen 'today or tomorrow'
items.summary: US treasury secretary says Hormuz deal with Iran could happen 'today or tomorrow' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the US could reach a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Wednesday, adding that this would stabilise energy prices. "We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC. He was optimistic about the impact a deal with Iran over the strait would have on energy prices, where he said hundreds of ships are waiting to pass. "Even though things are still a little dicey there over the past few days, we've [seen] quite a few ships coming out even now," Bessent said. "So, you know, I'd expect the energy prices to settle back down, which, as I said, will be good for the entire world."

A senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and prolific historian, Kagan has advocated U.S. primacy for decades, starting with his support for Nicaragua’s Contra insurgents as the head of the State Department’s Office of Public Diplomacy (1985-88). In 1997, Kagan co-founded Project for the New American Century, a neoconservative think tank that lobbied for a muscular foreign policy and the maintenance of U.S. global hegemony. The group exercised its considerable influence to push regime change in Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. Kagan’s advocacy has always been based on a belief that the world would collapse into disorder without American leadership, even though U.S. military misadventures have repeatedly destabilized parts of the world. So, is Robert Kagan now reconsidering his past hawkishness? I interview

items.title: US is the real loser if Senate passes virtue signaling Russia sanctions
items.summary: As the Senate returns to Washington for its last week in session until mid-September, it faces a long to-do list. But for many senators, the top priority is not enacting legislation that will help Americans but instead rushing to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 , known colloquially as the “Russia sanctions bill.” A passion project of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The legislation’s backers hope that, by choking off funding for Russia’s war effort, they can force Moscow to make greater concessions in ongoing negotiations to end the four-year old conflict in Ukraine. But this logic and the bill itself are fundamentally flawed. The new legislation will have a limited effect on Russia’s fortunes; as has been the case since the beginning of the war, additional economic punishments are unlikely to be decisive in Putin’s calculus. items.title: The collapse of national sovereignty in the Middle East
items.summary: Those who anticipated that a U.S. war against Iran would risk igniting a region-wide conflagration are looking prescient. The latest metastasis of the conflict has included airstrikes by both the United States and Saudi Arabia in Iraq, against Iraqi militias seen as allied with Iran. The Houthi regime in Yemen, as a direct outgrowth of the U.S.-Iran war, has renewed attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. This has led to new fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which is preparing a possible new offensive in Yemen and is attempting to draw in dozens of other countries on its side of this fray. The Iranian strategy of responding to the U.S. and Israeli aggression through horizontal escalation has drawn in still more countries. Iranian strikes against Saudi Arabia and the UAE have led to Saudi and Emirati attacks in Iran. Other Iranian retaliatory strikes have occurred in Kuwait , Bahrain , Qatar , and Jordan , scene of the most recent American casualties. items.title: Fox News screaming desperately into wind as Trump loses grip
items.summary: Fox News has always served as a purveyor of Republican war propaganda, but its coverage of the Iran conflict has been particularly aggressive, and in many ways unmoored from reality, giving their viewers a more than skewed vision of what President Donald Trump can — and cannot — accomplish in Iran today. It appears that it has been an editorial decision at Fox to convince their audience (whose median age is 55) that the Iranians cannot be negotiated with nor trusted and that war was — and still is — the only option. Its range of hosts and guests continue to insist that Trump’s military campaign has been a rousing success (by all independent, observable accounts it has not) and he just needs to finish the job. items.title: US, Israel to hold off on Iran strikes
items.summary: US President Donald Trump has pulled back from plans for major new strikes on Iran, in his latest climbdown after weeks of threatening to hit Tehran hard. The president said late Saturday that the US would hold off, provided a deal can be reached quickly. It follows a phone call with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who reportedly urged de-escalation, amid fears that Iran could retaliate against the Kingdom and other Gulf states. In announcing that he was calling off the strikes, Trump said Israel had “joined him in this commitment”. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has yet to comment. items.title: Decades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakes | Simon Tisdall
items.summary: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history It’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hosts reimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist rule after regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword for ill-considered western interventionism and nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase first coined during Vietnam . If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. items.title: MBS and Trump talk over the phone
items.summary: MBS and Trump talk over the phone Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has spoken to US President Donald Trump over the phone on developments in the region. According to Saudi state media, the crown prince stressed "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce, which paves the way for diplomatic solutions". He also said diplomatic solutions should "yield positive results for preserving the security and stability of the region and prevent it from being drawn into a wider conflict". This comes after Saudi Arabia expressed concern over Trump's plans for massive strikes against Iran, which have now apparently been cancelled, on Saturday.

items.title: Former Israeli prime minister vows to declare Qatar ‘enemy’ if elected
items.summary: Former Israeli prime minister vows to declare Qatar ‘enemy’ if elected Former prime minister Naftali Bennett has vowed to declare Qatar as an “enemy” if elected into government later this year, saying “it is unforgivable” that this is not already the case. In an interview with Channel 12, Bennett described Qatar as “more dangerous” to Israel at the moment than Iran. “With Iran, everyone knows that [it says], ‘We’ll destroy Israel.’” But Qatar, he said, “funded the Nukhba terrorists of October 7 [2023]… Qatar operates Al Jazeera, which is the most poisonous cancer hurting us.” “Qatar reaches places of influence in American universities… And most importantly, [it has access] to the most sacred place for the security of Israel — that is the office of the prime minister of Israel,” he said. "Qatar works against us and poisons us from within,” Bennett said, fuming that Israel does not define Qatar as an enemy state.

items.title: US embassies tell citizens to 'consider departing' Middle East
items.summary: US embassies tell citizens to 'consider departing' Middle East US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts urging American citizens to "consider departing" the region due to "the potential for an unforseen escalation" in the conflict between the US and Iran. The warnings come after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "very hard" on Friday amid widespread US media reports anticipating an escalation in US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure. "Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions," said an alert circulated by the US embassy in Jordan, with versions of the same text also posted by the American missions in Jerusalem, Muscat, Baghdad and Beirut. Americans in Jordan were also advised to avoid travel to military bases in the country and to "exercise caution and stay alert at locations publicly associated with the United States."

items.title: The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi
items.summary: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow The US war against Iran is spiraling out of control. Over the past week, the conflict has expanded across the Middle East , with attacks and counterattacks in at least five other countries. Instead of a quick war that sought to topple Iran’s regime, Donald Trump has started a regional conflict that risks severely disrupting energy supplies and prices – and triggering a global recession. After a few days of relative calm, the conflict resumed with the Pentagon carrying out almost nightly strikes against Iran, and Tehran retaliating against US military bases in the region. The conflict also extended to attacks in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan and Egypt. And there’s little sign that peace negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being brokered by Pakistan and Qatar, are making much progress. Continue reading...

items.summary: Kpler says Hormuz traffic drops sharply, remains steady through Bab el-Mandeb Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped sharply, with vessel crossings falling 77 percent day-on-day to just five ships, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler. Kpler said all recorded transits used the Iranian Unilateral Scheme, indicating reduced operational confidence and limited routing options through the strategic waterway. By contrast, traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb remained relatively steady, with 47 vessel crossings despite continued movements by sanctioned ships, shadow fleet activity, and one dark transit. "With US and Iranian public positions still at odds, operators are closely monitoring traffic volumes, routing behaviour and any diplomatic developments that could reshape risk across regional shipping lanes in the days ahead," Kpler said. items.title: The 'Board of Peace' announced a Palestinian body will take Hamas weapons. That's not what Trump said
items.summary: The 'Board of Peace' announced a Palestinian body will take Hamas weapons. items.title: Biosecurity Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: As part of its coverage of disruptive technologies that might come to pose global-scale threats, the Bulletin publishes articles on all the ways in which emerging science and technology can affect biological risks. COVID-19 highlighted those risks and led to voluminous coverage of the pandemic and related subjects, including gain-of-function research that could create potentially dangerous new pathogens that might, if accidentally released, spark a disease outbreak. But we also attempt to answer a wide variety of biosecurity- and biosafety-related questions: Are the laboratories used to study pathogens as safe and secure as they need to be? Will artificial intelligence make it easier and simpler for bad actors to develop or use biological weapons? Will efforts at human enhancement spark arms races or exacerbate societal inequality? Do policies that reduce compulsory vaccination increase the threat of diseases once thought tamed? Can political disinformation about bioweapons disrupt international efforts to minimize threats?

items.summary: Last month, as world leaders prepared to gather in France for the G7 Summit, French officials had Donald Trump on the mind. Using its privileges as host, Paris worked diligently to avoid any hiccups that might upset the U.S. president. First, it delayed the meeting from June 14 to June 16, ensuring that it wouldn’t interfere with Trump’s 80th birthday celebration, or the cage match on the White House lawn that accompanied it. Then, French President Emmanuel Macron went “out of his way” to design an agenda to “appeal to the sort of things Trump wants,” as one analyst told Reuters. Last, and perhaps most bizarrely, French officials delayed the ceremonial transfer of the remains of French Resistance hero Marc Bloch, who was set to be reinterred at France’s illustrious Panthéon in the heart of Paris on June 16. One of the most consequential questions raised by the various bills is whether to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force that has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since 2023, as a terrorist group. What effects could a terrorist designation for the RSF have? And would a designation constrain the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which is credibly accused of backing the RSF? items.title: Party elites so blind they can't see their base turning against the war
items.summary: Last week, only four House Republicans voted with 210 Democrats to pass a war powers resolution to end the U.S. war with Iran. That means 208 House Republicans voted to continue the war. Hours later, the Republican-led Senate killed the measure, with only one GOP senator voting with the Democrats to end the war, de facto joining four other Republicans who were either absent or missed the vote. The overwhelming majority of congressional Republicans are still clearly committed to President Donald Trump’s war. Republican voters? Not so much. A new Politico poll , published just one day before these votes, revealed a growing gap between congressional Republicans’ continued unqualified support for the war and GOP voters' seeming increasing lack of it. As recently as May, “half of President Donald Trump’s MAGA base thought the Iran war was worth its economic costs” but now barely over a third do, the news outlet reported. items.title: Iran holds funeral for pilot killed during March mission
items.summary: Iran holds funeral for pilot killed during March mission Funeral ceremonies have begun in Iran for air force pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during a combat mission in March. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei paid tribute to the second brigadier general after authorities recovered and identified his remains. Kazemi was one of four crew members aboard two Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force Su-24 bombers taking part in an attack on 2 March 2026. Iranian military officials said air defence systems struck the aircraft while they were flying over the Gulf. Baghaei said search operations and identification efforts remained under way for the other three crew members. He announced the funeral processions in a statement on X as mourners gathered to honour Kazemi.

items.title: Support for Israeli-US war on Iran falls as most Americans call it pointless
items.summary: Support for Israeli-US war on Iran falls as most Americans call it pointless Public backing in the United States for the war on Iran has continued to weaken, a new poll has found. About two-thirds of US adults said the conflict which Israel pushed the country in to had no purpose and was not worth pursuing, the survey by the Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research showed. The findings also indicated declining support for President Donald Trump’s decision to wage war, with few respondents favouring a prolonged conflict. Only two in 10 adults supported continuing US military operations against Iran. Three in 10 said Washington should halt its attacks and pursue another ceasefire through negotiations. The results point to growing public opposition as the war continues to drain US military resources, increase fuel costs, and destabilise the wider Middle East.

items.title: IRGC says it downed hostile drone over southwestern Iran
items.summary: IRGC says it downed hostile drone over southwestern Iran Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone over the southwestern port city of Bandar Imam Khomeini early on Thursday. The IRGC’s local division detected the unmanned aircraft inside the city’s airspace before shooting it down, the Tasnim news agency reported. Parts of the drone fell onto a residential property following the interception, but authorities reported no deaths. An IRGC explosives team later secured the wreckage, removed it from the house and neutralised any remaining danger, Tasnim said. The military did not identify the drone’s type, origin or intended target. Bandar Imam Khomeini sits on the Gulf coast in Iran’s Khuzestan province and contains one of the country’s most important commercial ports.

items.title: Iran blames US for Hormuz closure as Oman talks continue
items.summary: Iran blames US for Hormuz closure as Oman talks continue Iran says negotiations with Oman remain under way in Tehran as efforts continue to address the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and disruption to global shipping. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Iranian and Omani officials had held several rounds of discussions since talks began last week, including further meetings on Thursday. Baghaei blamed US and Israeli military operations for destabilising the vital waterway. “What is clear is that currently, the Strait of Hormuz is closed due to American actions and the insecurity that America has imposed on this waterway,” Baghaei told the ILNA news agency. “International shipping is being harmed and damaged solely because of American actions.”

items.title: Nuclear Risk Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: Founded by scientists and engineers of the Manhattan Project in the wake of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists has been alerting humanity to the danger of nuclear catastrophe since December 1945. For 80 years, the Bulletin has relentlessly pursued this mission by informing the public, policymakers, and scientists about new and evolving risks from nuclear technologies. Our authors include the world’s leading experts in the fields of nuclear weapons and their delivery platforms, nuclear security, nuclear safety, and nuclear waste policy. These experts and a staff of editors work together to provide accessible, authoritative articles for policy makers and citizens alike, with the aim of ensuring that nuclear science makes life on Earth better, not worse.

items.summary: IRGC says missiles destroyed three US F-35 jets at Jordan base Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it fired several ballistic missiles at Jordan’s al-Azraq airbase, which hosts US F-35 fighter jets. The IRGC said the attack targeted a runway and maintenance hangar in response to a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island that killed two parents and their child, the Fars news agency reported. It said the missiles completely destroyed three F-35 aircraft and inflicted “heavy damage” on three others. The IRGC also said the attack killed several officers and members of the base’s technical and maintenance teams. “A number of enemy officers and technical and maintenance personnel were also killed in this attack. Our region is no place for the infanticidal army that cruelly slaughters innocent families in the middle of the night while they sleep,” it said. The group said its struggle, alongside Jordan’s, would continue until “the last American occupier is expelled from the Islamic lands”.

items.summary: US awards Lockheed Martin $58.6bn Patriot missile contract The US Army has awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6bn to expand production of Patriot interceptor missiles, the Reuters news agency reported. The seven-year agreement will run from the 2026 financial year until 2032 as Washington seeks to rebuild weapons stockpiles depleted by its war on Iran and military support for Ukraine. items.title: Egypt says drone attack sparked fire on American LNG ships
items.summary: Egypt says drone attack sparked fire on American LNG ships Egypt has attributed a fire that damaged two vessels at the Mediterranean port of Damietta to a drone attack, marking its first official account of Wednesday’s incident. The Egyptian cabinet said preliminary findings showed that a drone caused the 29 July blaze. No group has taken responsibility. Authorities have opened an investigation into the circumstances of the attack, citing the need to defend Egypt’s national security and interests. Maritime security company Ambrey said the drone struck a US-owned floating gas storage tanker before flames spread to a second vessel. Officials reported no casualties. Egypt’s Petroleum Ministry had previously confirmed the fire but did not identify its cause. The attack has raised fears that the regional war could spread further after Iran targeted US-linked interests in several countries. If confirmed as part of the wider conflict, it would represent the first attack of its kind on Egyptian territory since the war began.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, openly enthusiastic, framed the event as paving the way toward “lasting peace and security” between Beirut and Tel Aviv. A month later, President Donald Trump received Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House. Once again, Rubio welcomed the visit and reiterated the goal of disarming Hezbollah and achieving a complete and definitive peace between Lebanon and its southern neighbor. Like Tel Aviv, Rubio favors a top-down approach that centers on force and coercion. To neutralize both Tehran and Hezbollah, this camp hopes to combine strong military action against Iranian territory with maximum pressure on the government in Beirut. The goal is two-fold: to strong-arm the Lebanese government into sidelining Hezbollah and to permanently separate the Lebanese and Iranian equations. items.title: Climate Change Archives - Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
items.summary: In 1978, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists published a cover story titled “Is mankind warming the Earth?” The answer then, as now, was an “unqualified ‘yes.’” Between July 2023 and June 2024, the average global temperature was over 1.5 degrees Celsius (or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the pre-industrial average, the result of over a century of rampant fossil fuel use and associated greenhouse gas emissions. This warming has resulted in global climate change. The Bulletin covers all aspects of the causes and wide-ranging impacts of this existential crisis, from glacier retreat and sea level rise to drought, extreme weather, and intense wildfires. We also investigate the most promising ways to slow and eventually halt global warming, probing uncertainties and irreversible tipping points in the Earth’s climate and biosphere that threatens all life on Earth.

AlBudaiwi described the attacks as a “dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of the kingdom’s sovereignty, and [is] a direct threat to its security and stability and to regional security and peace”. items.title: Ships stuck in strait of Hormuz pose ‘super-spreader’ biodiversity threat, scientists warn
items.summary: Biologists say cargo ships stranded in Gulf may carry highly potent invasive species around the world as trade resumes The closure of the strait of Hormuz has created conditions for an extreme global biodiversity threat, with scientists warning that thousands of stranded ships could spread invasive marine species across the world’s oceans once they begin sailing again. More than 1,500 commercial vessels have been stuck in the Gulf since the strategic waterway closed on 28 February after the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran . An international team of marine biologists said that with the stranded ships remaining motionless, their hulls were becoming encrusted with marine life – from microbes and algae to barnacles and other invertebrates – that could hitchhike to ports around the world when trade resumed. items.title: Trump hails late US Senator Lindsey Graham as 'true American original'
items.summary: Trump hails late US Senator Lindsey Graham as 'true American original' World leaders gathered in Washington, DC, on Tuesday for the funeral ceremony for late Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham, who was instrumental in advocating for the war on Iran and a staunch supporter of Israel. Among those attending were Ukrainian President Zelensky and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. Delivering remarks at the ceremony, Trump called Graham a "beloved friend" and "a true American original". "He never saw a war that he didn’t like," Trump said, drawing laughter before adding that Graham supported military power "for the good of our country." "Above all, Lindsey Graham believed in a strong America," Trump said. "He had unwavering faith in the righteousness of American power." US President Donald Trump delivers remarks during the funeral service for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham at the Washington National Cathedral, on 28 July 2026 (AFP)

items.title: Iran proposes temporary Hormuz plan to give itself more control over transit
items.summary: Iran proposes temporary Hormuz plan to give itself more control over transit Iran has proposed to Oman a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, under which one direction of traffic and part of the traffic in the opposite direction would pass through Iranian waters, allowing for greater Iranian control of transit. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state TV on Tuesday that Tehran rejected an Omani proposal for an equal division of transit routes between the two countries, saying that it did not address Iran’s security concerns amid ongoing US-Israeli attacks on the country. He said that if Muscat rejected Iran’s proposal, the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed, adding that Tehran had never recognised the alternative southern route along Oman’s coast.
